# EFS and FSx: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q015 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a short-lived high performance computing (HPC) simulation on Amazon EC2 Linux instances for two weeks. The input data is in an Amazon S3 bucket, and the results must be written back to the bucket. The simulation needs a file system with very high throughput. If a file server fails, the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Create an FSx for Lustre persistent file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups of the file system.
- Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and turn on daily automatic backups to protect the results.
- Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with Provisioned throughput, and copy the input data from the bucket before the job starts.
- Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and export the results to the bucket when the job ends.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, and export the results to the bucket when the job ends.

**Deciding phrases.** "short-lived", "the job can read the input from Amazon S3 again and repeat the failed step", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution.
2. I mark the constraints: the job is short-lived, the input is in Amazon S3, the results go back to the bucket, the job needs very high throughput, and it can repeat a failed step.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket, because scratch is cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads.
4. I remove both options with daily backups: backups are not supported on scratch file systems, and not on file systems linked to Amazon S3. I remove Amazon EFS, because FSx for Lustre is the file system built for HPC, and the EFS option copies the whole input first.
5. Between the persistent file system and the scratch file system, the difference is replication; the stem says the job can read its input from Amazon S3 again, so I do not pay for replicated data.
6. Check: the scratch file system linked to the bucket meets every constraint, and it writes the results back to the bucket. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The job is short-lived, and it can repeat a failed step from the data in Amazon S3. On a scratch file system the [data is not replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-scratch-temporary-not-replicated), which this job accepts. The link to the bucket [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), so the job starts without a full copy.

**Why not.**

- "Create an FSx for Lustre persistent file system ...": This configuration does not exist: backups are [supported only on FSx for Lustre persistent](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-backups-persistent-only-not-s3-linked-not-scratch) file systems [not linked to an Amazon S3 data repository](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-backups-persistent-only-not-s3-linked-not-scratch). Its [data is replicated](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-persistent-replicated-servers-replaced) too, which this job does not need.
- "Create an FSx for Lustre scratch file system ...": [Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-scratch), so this configuration does not exist.
- "Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with ...": FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and this option adds a full copy of the input before the job can start.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the results stay on the file system for months, and the job is sensitive to downtime" instead: a persistent file system, because it fits workloads [sensitive to disruptions in availability](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term).

**Takeaway.** A short HPC job that can rerun from S3: FSx for Lustre scratch, linked to the bucket.

**Review.** [FSx for Lustre feeds compute-heavy jobs and loads S3 data on first access](2-deep.md#fsx-for-lustre-feeds-compute-heavy-jobs-and-loads-s3-data-on-first-access-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs on-premises ZFS file servers that Linux applications access over NFS. Several times each day, test teams create writable copies of production volumes from ZFS snapshots, and scripts automate this workflow. The company wants to migrate the file servers to AWS without changing the application code or the way the teams create these copies. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Migrate the data to Amazon EFS, back up the file system with AWS Backup, and restore a recovery point to a new file system each time a team needs a copy.
- Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and create a writable clone volume from a point-in-time snapshot each time a team needs a copy.
- Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror, and create a volume from a SnapMirror copy each time a team needs a copy.
- Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to an Amazon S3 bucket, and copy a production folder to a new directory each time a team needs a copy.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and create a writable clone volume from a point-in-time snapshot each time a team needs a copy.

**Deciding phrases.** "ZFS file servers", "writable copies of production volumes from ZFS snapshots", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the migration with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: ZFS file servers, Linux clients over NFS, writable copies from snapshots several times a day, and no change to the applications or to the copy workflow.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon EFS, because it is the shared NFS file system for Linux clients on AWS.
4. I remove FSx for Lustre, because a folder copy is not a snapshot clone, and Lustre is built for machine learning and HPC. I remove FSx for NetApp ONTAP with SnapMirror, because AWS recommends SnapMirror to migrate NetApp ONTAP file systems, and these servers run ZFS.
5. Between Amazon EFS with AWS Backup and FSx for OpenZFS the difference is the copy workflow. My first idea breaks because each EFS copy becomes a full restore, while FSx for OpenZFS offers point-in-time snapshots and in-place data cloning, and AWS recommends it for ZFS servers.
6. Check: FSx for OpenZFS keeps NFS for the applications, and a clone is a writable copy created almost instantly from a snapshot. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** ZFS servers and writable copies from snapshots decide this question. AWS recommends [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs) when the current storage is ZFS, and it lets you migrate [without changing your applications](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-overview-openzfs-migrate-without-changing-apps). It offers [point-in-time snapshots, in-place data cloning](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-openzfs-snapshots-clones-replication), and a clone is a [writable copy](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot), so the teams keep their workflow.

**Why not.**

- "Migrate the data to Amazon EFS, back up ...": It works, but each copy is a full restore with a wait and an extra file system, and AWS recommends [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs) for ZFS servers.
- "Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for NetApp ...": AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp), but the source is ZFS, and the teams would change their snapshot and clone workflow.
- "Migrate the data to Amazon FSx for Lustre ...": FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and a folder copy replaces the teams' snapshot and clone workflow.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a NetApp ONTAP system that serves NFS and SMB clients" instead: choose FSx for NetApp ONTAP, because AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp).

**Takeaway.** ZFS servers with snapshots and clones move to FSx for OpenZFS; NetApp systems move to FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

**Review.** [FSx for OpenZFS moves ZFS and Linux NFS servers with snapshots and clones](2-deep.md#fsx-for-openzfs-moves-zfs-and-linux-nfs-servers-with-snapshots-and-clones-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must read and write the same set of files at the same time. The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
- Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
- Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
- Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS", "without changing the application", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Linux clients that share files over NFS fit Amazon EFS. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), and each zone gets a mount target, so both zones read and write the same files. AWS runs the storage, so the company has no file server to patch.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server ...": It serves files over [the SMB protocol](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-windows-smb-protocol) and needs an Active Directory domain, which the Linux NFS clients do not use.
- "Install file server software on a new EC2 ...": It can work, but the company runs and patches the file server itself, while EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning).
- "Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach ...": Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory" instead: FSx for Windows File Server, because EFS on Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).

**Takeaway.** Linux instances that share files over NFS across zones: Amazon EFS.

**Review.** [Amazon EFS gives many Linux clients one shared file system over NFS](2-deep.md#amazon-efs-gives-many-linux-clients-one-shared-file-system-over-nfs-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a serverless document-processing application. Many AWS Lambda functions run at the same time, and all of them must read and update the same set of files with standard file operations. The files must persist between invocations and must be visible to every function. The functions already connect to a VPC in one AWS Region. Which storage solution meets these requirements?

- Write the files to the /tmp directory of each function, and read the files back from /tmp in later invocations.
- Create an Amazon EBS gp3 volume, and attach the volume to each function when the function starts to process a request.
- Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount targets in the VPC, and configure each function to mount the file system.
- Store the files as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket, and read and write the objects with the S3 API from each function.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EFS file system with mount targets in the VPC, and configure each function to mount the file system.

**Deciding phrases.** "the same set of files with standard file operations", "persist between invocations", "visible to every function"

**Why.** Many functions need one shared set of files with standard file operations. You can access EFS from Lambda by referencing [an EFS file system in your function settings](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings), and the function reaches it [over the local network in a VPC](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-efs-shared-mount-in-vpc). The files stay in EFS between invocations.

**Why not.**

- "Write the files to the /tmp directory of ...": /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment), so other functions do not see the files, and the files are not guaranteed to persist.
- "Create an Amazon EBS gp3 volume, and attach ...": Block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), so it is not a file system that many functions share.
- "Store the files as objects in an Amazon ...": S3 is an [object storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), so the code uses API calls instead of the standard file operations that the stem requires.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each function needs scratch space for one invocation only" instead: the /tmp directory, because /tmp is [temporary and unique to each execution environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-unique-per-environment).

**Takeaway.** Lambda functions that share files and keep them between invocations mount Amazon EFS.

**Review.** [Amazon EFS gives many Linux clients one shared file system over NFS](2-deep.md#amazon-efs-gives-many-linux-clients-one-shared-file-system-over-nfs-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company stores about 100 GiB of application data on an Amazon EFS Regional file system that uses Bursting throughput. The file system has used all of its burst credits, and the application slows down. The throughput is spiky and unpredictable: the application is idle most of the day, then drives short peaks. The company must restore the performance of the application. Which change will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.
- Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and set the provisioned level to the throughput that the application needs at its peak.
- Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data in the file system to raise the baseline throughput that the file system earns.
- Create a new file system that uses the Max I/O performance mode, and copy the application data to the new file system.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Switch the file system to Elastic throughput, so that throughput scales up and down with the reads and writes of the application.

**Deciding phrases.** "spiky and unpredictable", "idle most of the day", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The file system ran out of burst credits, and its load is spiky and unpredictable. Elastic throughput [scales automatically](../facts/efs.md#efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use), so the short peaks get the throughput that they need. The company pays for the reads and writes, not for a level that stays unused through the idle hours.

**Why not.**

- "Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput, and ...": It works, but you are [charged for the amount of throughput enabled](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-billed-for-throughput-enabled) all day, although the application is idle most of the time.
- "Keep Bursting throughput, and store extra unused data ...": Bursting gives [throughput that scales with the amount of storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-bursting-scales-with-storage-size-recommended-for), so the company pays to store data that nobody reads.
- "Create a new file system that uses the ...": Max I/O changes the performance mode, not the throughput mode, and AWS recommends [always using General Purpose performance mode](../facts/efs.md#efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The application drives a steady-state, predictable throughput close to its peak all day" instead: Provisioned throughput, because it fits [predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained).

**Takeaway.** Spiky or unpredictable EFS throughput: Elastic throughput, which charges for what the application uses.

**Review.** [Elastic throughput follows the workload and Provisioned throughput follows your setting](2-deep.md#elastic-throughput-follows-the-workload-and-provisioned-throughput-follows-your-setting-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
- Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
- Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
- Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.

**Deciding phrases.** "development build artifacts that the team can re-create", "a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The team can re-create the files, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), and AWS names them for [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases). One zone is the cheapest fit. Backups do not decide it; from the CLI they are [enabled by default only for One Zone](../facts/efs.md#efs-backup-cli-api-default-only-one-zone).

**Why not.**

- "Create an EFS Regional file system that stores ...": It works, but it pays for availability that the stem does not need, because One Zone fits applications that [do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability](../facts/efs.md#efs-pricing-one-zone-for-no-multi-az-need).
- "Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure ...": It works, but it adds a second file system in a [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice) for files that the team can re-create.
- "Create two EFS One Zone file systems in ...": Two file systems and a sync task cost more than one One Zone file system, and the stem accepts a loss of access during a zone outage.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails" instead: a Regional file system, because it gives [continuous availability to the data](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability).

**Takeaway.** Re-creatable development files and an accepted zone outage: EFS One Zone.

**Review.** [A Regional file system survives a zone failure but One Zone does not](2-deep.md#a-regional-file-system-survives-a-zone-failure-but-one-zone-does-not-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company is moving an application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must read and write the same set of files at the same time. The instances run Windows Server, and users reach the files through SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory. The company wants to move the files from its data center to AWS without changing the application. Which storage solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount the file system on every instance.
- Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.
- Install file server software on a new EC2 instance with a large Amazon EBS volume, and share the files from it with every instance.
- Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to every instance in both Availability Zones.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system that is joined to Active Directory, and map its share on every instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "The instances run Windows Server", "SMB shares with permissions from the company's Active Directory", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Windows Server instances that use SMB shares with Active Directory permissions fit FSx for Windows File Server. The domain provides [user authentication and file- and folder-level access control](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls), so the shares keep their permissions. AWS manages the file servers, so the company patches nothing.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon EFS file system with a ...": Using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported), so the Windows Server instances cannot use the file system.
- "Install file server software on a new EC2 ...": It can work, but the company runs and patches the Windows file server itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).
- "Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach ...": Multi-Attach attaches one io2 volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the instances in the second zone cannot attach it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The instances run Linux and access the files over NFS" instead: Amazon EFS, because it serves EC2 instances [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).

**Takeaway.** Windows instances, SMB shares and Active Directory permissions: FSx for Windows File Server.

**Review.** [FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB shares that join your Active Directory](2-deep.md#fsx-for-windows-file-server-serves-smb-shares-that-join-your-active-directory-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs a Linux application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The instances share a set of files through an Amazon EFS file system. The files are production reports, and the file system must be highly available if one Availability Zone fails. The company plans to create a new file system for these files. Which file system configuration will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Create an EFS One Zone file system in one Availability Zone, and keep the automatic backups of the new file system turned on.
- Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.
- Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure EFS Replication to a destination file system in a second AWS Region.
- Create two EFS One Zone file systems in two Availability Zones, and keep them in sync with a scheduled AWS DataSync task.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an EFS Regional file system that stores data across Availability Zones, and create a mount target in each zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "production reports", "highly available if one Availability Zone fails", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The stem asks for files that stay available when a zone fails. A Regional file system stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-recommended-type), so the instances reach the data through the mount targets in the other zones. One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-single-az), so a zone outage stops access.

**Why not.**

- "Create an EFS One Zone file system in ...": One Zone is [not resilient to a complete AZ outage](../facts/efs.md#efs-onezone-not-resilient-to-az-outage), and a backup restores the files later instead of keeping them available.
- "Create an EFS Regional file system, and configure ...": It works, but a Regional file system is designed to [sustain data if an AZ is lost](../facts/efs.md#efs-regional-designed-to-sustain-az-loss), so a replica in a second Region adds cost that the stem does not ask for.
- "Create two EFS One Zone file systems in ...": A scheduled copy runs behind the source, and someone switches the instances to the other file system after a zone fails.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The files are development build artifacts that the team can re-create, and a loss of access during an Availability Zone outage is acceptable" instead: One Zone, because it suits [development, build, and staging environments](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases).

**Takeaway.** Files that stay available through a zone failure: an EFS Regional file system, not One Zone.

**Review.** [A Regional file system survives a zone failure but One Zone does not](2-deep.md#a-regional-file-system-survives-a-zone-failure-but-one-zone-does-not-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A media company stores project files on an Amazon EFS file system that Linux editing servers mount. The files of each project are read often for about one month and then become infrequently accessed. Months later, an old project is sometimes reopened, and its files are then read many times each day by editors who need low latency. The company wants to reduce storage cost without changing the application. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after 30 days without access and moves files back to EFS Standard on their first access.
- Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after 30 days without access, because files that are read again return to EFS Standard by default.
- Copy files older than 30 days to an Amazon S3 bucket, and add an S3 Lifecycle rule that moves objects back to S3 Standard when an editor reads them again.
- Keep every file in the EFS Standard storage class and create no lifecycle policy, so that the files of reopened projects keep the lowest latency for every read.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after 30 days without access and moves files back to EFS Standard on their first access.

**Deciding phrases.** "infrequently accessed", "read many times each day by editors who need low latency", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Files turn cold after a month, but a reopened project needs low latency again. EFS IA offers [up to 95% lower cost](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-ia-cost-95-percent) than EFS Standard for data read [a few times a quarter](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for). By default, read files are [not moved back to the Standard storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard), so the policy also needs to [transition files into Standard storage](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-transition-to-standard-on-first-access) on first access.

**Why not.**

- "Create a lifecycle policy that moves files to ...": By default, read files are [not moved back to the Standard storage class](../facts/efs.md#efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard), so reopened projects stay in EFS IA with [tens of milliseconds](../facts/efs.md#efs-latency-ia-archive-first-byte) of first-byte latency.
- "Copy files older than 30 days to an ...": The servers read files through a mounted file system, and Amazon S3 is an [object storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), so this changes the application.
- "Keep every file in the EFS Standard storage ...": It works, but cold files stay in the most expensive class, while EFS IA offers [up to 95% lower cost](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-ia-cost-95-percent) for files that are read rarely.

**Twin.** If the stem said "old projects are never reopened, and a slow first read is acceptable" instead: also move files to EFS Archive, which is designed for data read [a few times a year or less](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for).

**Takeaway.** EFS IA cuts the cost of cold files; add Transition into Standard when old files can become hot again.

**Review.** [Cold files move to cheaper classes and stay there unless you ask](2-deep.md#cold-files-move-to-cheaper-classes-and-stay-there-unless-you-ask-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q010 -->
### Question 10

A company runs a reporting web application on Linux Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group that spans three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. The application saves each generated report as a file in a local directory. Users share report links with colleagues, and many downloads fail because the request reaches an instance that does not hold the file. Instances are added and removed during the day. The fix must need minimal code changes. What should a solutions architect do?

- Turn on sticky sessions for the target group, so that the load balancer sends each user's requests to the instance that created that user's reports.
- Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume at the report directory of every instance in the group.
- Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, so that each instance finishes its open downloads before the group removes the instance.
- Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount it at the report directory on every instance.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each Availability Zone, and mount it at the report directory on every instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "the request reaches an instance that does not hold the file", "Instances are added and removed during the day", "minimal code changes"

**Why.** Each report lives on one instance, and [data is not automatically copied](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances) to instances that the group launches. An EFS file system mounted at the report directory is shared [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs) in several Availability Zones, so every instance sees every report. EFS [requires no changes to your existing applications](../facts/efs.md#efs-overview-regional-linux-shared-access), because the application still writes to a directory.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on sticky sessions for the target group, ...": Stickiness can [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but a colleague's request can reach another instance, and a removed instance takes its reports with it.
- "Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach ...": Multi-Attach attaches one volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so it cannot serve a group that spans three zones.
- "Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, ...": A longer delay lets open requests finish, but each report still lives on one instance, so requests that reach other instances still fail.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each user downloads only the reports that the user created, and instances are never removed" instead: sticky sessions could work, because they [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what).

**Takeaway.** Files that every instance of an Auto Scaling group reads belong on a shared EFS file system, not on one instance.

**Review.** [Amazon EFS gives many Linux clients one shared file system over NFS](2-deep.md#amazon-efs-gives-many-linux-clients-one-shared-file-system-over-nfs-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q012 -->
### Question 11

A company is migrating an application to AWS. A PostgreSQL database runs on one Amazon EC2 instance and needs durable, low-latency block storage for a moderate, steady I/O load. Six Linux web instances in three Availability Zones must read and write the same set of uploaded files. The company does not want to copy files between instances. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)

- Store the database files on the Amazon EFS file system that the web instances also mount for the uploaded files.
- Store the database on an Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume that is attached to the database instance.
- Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on and attached to all six web instances.
- Store the database on an Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volume with the highest IOPS level that the instance supports.
- Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each of the three Availability Zones.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Store the database on an Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume that is attached to the database instance.
- Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EFS file system with a mount target in each of the three Availability Zones.

**Deciding phrases.** "runs on one Amazon EC2 instance", "moderate, steady I/O load", "three Availability Zones must read and write the same set of uploaded files", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The database needs block storage on one instance; the uploads need one set of files that six instances share across three zones. EBS is a [block-level storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object), and EFS is a [file storage service](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object) that instances use [concurrently from multiple NFS clients](../facts/efs.md#efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs).

- Block storage is for durable, low-latency storage [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance), such as databases, and AWS lists gp3 for [medium sized single instance databases](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-use-cases).
- File system storage gives [shared read and write access](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-file-system-row-shared-access) across instances, and one EFS file system serves clients in all three Availability Zones.

**Why not.**

- "Store the database files on the Amazon EFS ...": The database runs on one instance, and EBS gives the [lowest-latency access to data](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-efs-vs-ebs-vs-s3) from a single instance; the database gains nothing from sharing.
- "Store the uploaded files on one Amazon EBS ...": Multi-Attach attaches a volume to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so one volume cannot serve web instances in three zones.
- "Store the database on an Amazon EBS Provisioned ...": It works, but gp3 is [the lowest cost SSD volume](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-gp3-lowest-cost-ssd) type, and io2 fits loads that need [higher IOPS and throughput than gp3 volumes](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-use-cases), which a moderate, steady load does not.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database needs sustained IOPS far above what gp3 delivers" instead: choose io2 for the database, because the IOPS need then decides the volume type.

**Takeaway.** One instance with a database: EBS block storage. Many instances in several zones that share files: EFS.

**Review.** [Amazon EFS gives many Linux clients one shared file system over NFS](2-deep.md#amazon-efs-gives-many-linux-clients-one-shared-file-system-over-nfs-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 12

A company runs Microsoft SQL Server failover cluster instances on Amazon EC2 instances that run Windows Server in two Availability Zones. The cluster needs shared storage over SMB for the database files. The storage must be highly available across the two Availability Zones and must give the low latency that a database needs. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with mount targets in both Availability Zones, and store the database files on the file system.
- Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage, and join it to the company's Active Directory domain.
- Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach turned on, and attach the volume to the cluster nodes in both Availability Zones.
- Create continuously available (CA) file shares on the FSx file system, and store the SQL Server data files and log files on those shares.
- Build a Windows file server cluster on two more EC2 instances in the two Availability Zones, and share their EBS volumes over SMB.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage, and join it to the company's Active Directory domain.
- Create continuously available (CA) file shares on the FSx file system, and store the SQL Server data files and log files on those shares.

**Deciding phrases.** "failover cluster instances", "shared storage over SMB", "highly available across the two Availability Zones", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The cluster needs SMB storage that both zones reach. FSx for Windows File Server can be [storage for active data files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-active-data-files-or-share-witness-ssd) of high availability SQL Server. A Multi-AZ file system keeps the shares available by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover).

- Multi-AZ uses [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication), and [SSD storage is recommended for SQL Server](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-sql-server-ssd-recommended).
- For SQL Server, AWS requires that you [use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server).

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon EFS Regional file system with ...": The cluster nodes run Windows Server, and using EFS with Windows instances [is not supported](../facts/efs.md#efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).
- "Create one Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach ...": Multi-Attach works for instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-multi-attach-provisioned-iops-same-az), so the node in the second zone cannot attach the volume.
- "Build a Windows file server cluster on two ...": It can work, but the team builds, patches and fails over the file servers itself, while FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

**Twin.** If the stem said "one SQL Server instance in one Availability Zone that uses block storage" instead: an Amazon EBS volume, because block storage is [attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers](../facts/efs.md#efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance).

**Takeaway.** SQL Server clusters across two zones on SMB: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ with SSD and CA shares.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ Windows file system fails over to a standby in another zone](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-windows-file-system-fails-over-to-a-standby-in-another-zone-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q014 -->
### Question 13

A research team trains machine learning models on a 200 TB dataset that is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The training runs on a cluster of Linux GPU instances that needs a shared file system with very high throughput. Each training job reads only part of the dataset, and training must start as soon as possible after the cluster launches. Trained models must be stored in the bucket. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that is linked to the bucket, start training at once, and export the trained models to the bucket.
- Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system, copy the whole dataset into it with an AWS DataSync task, and start training after the copy completes.
- Create an Amazon EFS file system, copy the dataset into it with an AWS DataSync task, and mount the file system on every GPU instance in the cluster.
- Download the part of the dataset that each job needs from the bucket to an Amazon EBS volume on every GPU instance when the instance boots.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system that is linked to the bucket, start training at once, and export the trained models to the bucket.

**Deciding phrases.** "very high throughput", "reads only part of the dataset", "as soon as possible", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** High throughput for machine learning and a fast start decide this question. FSx for Lustre is built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads). Linked to the bucket, it [transparently presents S3 objects as files](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), and content is [imported automatically from S3 only when you access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access) a file, so training starts without a bulk copy.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system, ...": It works, but the bulk copy delays training and adds a task, while content is [imported automatically from S3 only when you access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access) a linked file.
- "Create an Amazon EFS file system, copy the ...": FSx for Lustre is the file system built for [machine learning, high-performance computing (HPC)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads), and the EFS copy also delays training until it completes.
- "Download the part of the dataset that each ...": Each instance gets a separate copy on its own volume, so the cluster has no shared file system, and every boot waits for a download.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Windows instances read the dataset over SMB" instead: choose FSx for Windows File Server, because AWS lists [Linux](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-client-compatibility) as the client of FSx for Lustre.

**Takeaway.** FSx for Lustre linked to S3 shows the bucket as files at once and loads content on first read.

**Review.** [FSx for Lustre feeds compute-heavy jobs and loads S3 data on first access](2-deep.md#fsx-for-lustre-feeds-compute-heavy-jobs-and-loads-s3-data-on-first-access-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q016 -->
### Question 14

A company stores production Windows file shares on one Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system that uses a Single-AZ deployment. Hundreds of employees map the shares over SMB every working day. The file shares must stay highly available if one Availability Zone fails, and failover must happen without manual steps. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Single-AZ 2 file system and move the shares to it, because a Single-AZ 2 file system fails over to another Availability Zone when its zone fails.
- Create a second Single-AZ file system in another Availability Zone, replicate the shares to it with a scheduled AWS DataSync task, and switch users after a failure.
- Create a Multi-AZ file system with a preferred file server and a standby file server in two Availability Zones, and move the shares to it.
- Keep the Single-AZ file system, take daily backups, and restore the latest backup to a new file system in another Availability Zone after a failure.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Multi-AZ file system with a preferred file server and a standby file server in two Availability Zones, and move the shares to it.

**Deciding phrases.** "highly available if one Availability Zone fails", "without manual steps", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem needs to survive a zone failure with automatic failover. A Multi-AZ deployment runs Windows file servers in [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication), with data [replicated synchronously within each individual AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication) and between the zones. It gives availability by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover), so employees keep their shares without manual steps.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Single-AZ 2 file system and move ...": A Single-AZ file system has a [single Windows file server instance](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime) in one zone and [about 30 minutes of downtime](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime) during recovery, with no standby elsewhere.
- "Create a second Single-AZ file system in another ...": You can use [AWS DataSync](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-windows-datasync-replicate-same-and-cross-region) for periodic replication to a second file system, but users switch by hand and lose changes since the last run.
- "Keep the Single-AZ file system, take daily backups, ...": A restore creates a new file system after the failure, so users wait for it and lose the changes made since the last backup.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a few hours of downtime are acceptable, and cost matters most" instead: keep a Single-AZ file system with daily backups, which runs a [single Windows file server instance](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime).

**Takeaway.** For zone failures, FSx for Windows File Server needs a Multi-AZ deployment; Single-AZ has one file server in one zone.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ Windows file system fails over to a standby in another zone](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-windows-file-system-fails-over-to-a-standby-in-another-zone-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q018 -->
### Question 15

A company wants to migrate an on-premises NetApp ONTAP storage system to AWS as a lift and shift. Linux applications use the data over NFS, and Windows users open the same volumes over SMB at the same time. The storage team already replicates volumes with NetApp SnapMirror and wants to keep its ONTAP tools. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Move the Linux data to Amazon EFS and the Windows data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and keep the two copies in sync with AWS DataSync.
- Move all data to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, and change the Linux applications so that they read and write the files over SMB.
- Move all data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and serve the same volumes to the Linux applications over NFS and to the Windows users over SMB.
- Migrate the volumes to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror, and serve the same volumes over NFS to Linux and over SMB to Windows.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Migrate the volumes to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror, and serve the same volumes over NFS to Linux and over SMB to Windows.

**Deciding phrases.** "the same volumes over SMB at the same time", "NetApp SnapMirror", "lift and shift", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** NFS and SMB on the same volumes, a lift and shift, and SnapMirror decide this question. FSx for NetApp ONTAP supports [all versions of the Network File System (NFS)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) and SMB, with [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) to the same data. AWS recommends SnapMirror to [migrate your NetApp ONTAP file systems](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp), so the team keeps its tools and one copy of the data.

**Why not.**

- "Move the Linux data to Amazon EFS and ...": It works, but two file systems and a sync job add overhead, while FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol) to one copy of the data.
- "Move all data to Amazon FSx for Windows ...": The Linux applications would need changes, which a lift and shift avoids, while FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves both protocols with [multi-protocol access](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol).
- "Move all data to Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, ...": AWS lists [NFS 3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-protocol-support) as the protocols of FSx for OpenZFS and no SMB, so the Windows users cannot open the volumes over SMB.

**Twin.** If the stem said "ZFS file servers that only Linux clients use over NFS" instead: choose [FSx for OpenZFS](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs), which AWS recommends for ZFS servers.

**Takeaway.** NFS and SMB on the same data, or a NetApp source: FSx for NetApp ONTAP, migrated with SnapMirror.

**Review.** [FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves NFS and SMB clients from the same data](2-deep.md#fsx-for-netapp-ontap-serves-nfs-and-smb-clients-from-the-same-data-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 16

A company keeps Windows home directories on one Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system with SSD storage. Employees map their home directories over SMB with permissions from the company's Active Directory. The data will grow to about 300 TiB within three years. Employees must keep using one share path, and the storage design must be scalable to that size. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the single file system, and increase its storage capacity every quarter so that it grows in place to hold all of the home directories.
- Move the home directories to one Amazon EFS file system, which grows automatically, and map it on the Windows clients as a network drive.
- Create several FSx for Windows File Server file systems, and group their file shares under one Microsoft DFS Namespaces namespace that employees map as one path.
- Run Windows file servers on Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon EBS volumes, and group their file shares under one Microsoft DFS Namespaces namespace.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create several FSx for Windows File Server file systems, and group their file shares under one Microsoft DFS Namespaces namespace that employees map as one path.

**Deciding phrases.** "about 300 TiB", "one share path", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A single file system has a [maximum storage capacity of single file system (64 TiB)](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), and the data will reach 300 TiB. DFS Namespaces groups the shares of several FSx for Windows File Server file systems into [one common folder structure, or namespace](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), so employees keep one path, and every file system stays fully managed.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the single file system, and increase its ...": One file system holds a maximum of [64 TiB](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity), so it cannot grow in place to 300 TiB of home directories.
- "Move the home directories to one Amazon EFS ...": EFS uses the [NFS v4](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-nfs-v4-protocol) protocol, not SMB with Active Directory permissions, so it does not serve these Windows home shares.
- "Run Windows file servers on Amazon EC2 instances ...": It works, but the company patches, backs up, and scales its own servers, while FSx for Windows File Server gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the data will grow to about 40 TiB" instead: increase the storage capacity of the one file system, which holds up to [64 TiB](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity).

**Takeaway.** One FSx for Windows File Server file system has a size limit; DFS Namespaces joins several under one path.

**Review.** [Windows file system storage grows in place but does not shrink](2-deep.md#windows-file-system-storage-grows-in-place-but-does-not-shrink-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q002 -->
### Question 17

A company runs Linux applications on Amazon EC2 instances that share an Amazon EFS file system. The company's on-premises data center connects to the VPC through an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. Linux servers in the data center must now mount the same file system, but every mount attempt times out. The security group of the mount targets allows inbound traffic only from the security group of the EC2 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

- Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from 0.0.0.0/0, and mount the file system by a mount target IP address.
- Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, give each mount target a public IP address, and allow TCP port 2049 from the public IP addresses of the data center.
- Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from the data center's address range, and mount by a mount target IP address.
- Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows HTTPS traffic on TCP port 443 from the data center's address range, and mount by a mount target IP address.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an inbound rule to the mount target security group that allows NFS traffic on TCP port 2049 from the data center's address range, and mount by a mount target IP address.

**Deciding phrases.** "every mount attempt times out", "allows inbound traffic only from the security group of the EC2 instances", "MOST secure"

**Why.** The timeout shows a network block: an NFS client [can only mount a file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) when it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) of a mount target. AWS says to [allow inbound traffic](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) to the [NFS port (2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049) from the server, and to mount by a [mount target IP address instead of](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-use-mount-target-ip-instead-of-dns) a DNS name. The data center's range keeps other networks out.

**Why not.**

- "Add an inbound rule to the mount target ...": It works, but every address that can reach the VPC can then try the NFS port, which is less secure than the data center's range.
- "Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, give ...": Servers on premises mount EFS when they connect over [AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-mount-via-direct-connect-or-vpn), which the company has, so internet exposure adds risk.
- "Add an inbound rule to the mount target ...": An NFS client [can only mount a file system](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049) when it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)](../facts/efs.md#efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049), so a rule for HTTPS leaves the mount blocked.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Windows servers in the data center" instead: no EFS rule helps, because an on-premises server [must have a Linux-based operating system](../facts/efs.md#efs-onpremises-server-must-be-linux); use FSx for Windows File Server.

**Takeaway.** Servers on premises mount EFS over VPN or Direct Connect after the mount target security group allows NFS from their range.

**Review.** [Each client reaches EFS through the mount target in its own Availability Zone](2-deep.md#each-client-reaches-efs-through-the-mount-target-in-its-own-availability-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=efs-fsx-q008 -->
### Question 18

A company is moving its Windows file shares from a file server in the company's data center to Amazon FSx for Windows File Server. Employees must keep signing in with their existing accounts, which live in the company's own Active Directory domain on domain controllers in the same data center. The data center connects to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect, and the domain controllers are reachable from the VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an AD Connector directory that points to the on-premises domain, and join the file system to the domain through the AD Connector directory.
- Join the file system directly to the existing on-premises domain as a self-managed Active Directory, using the domain's DNS servers and a service account.
- Create a Simple AD directory in the VPC, copy the employees' user accounts into it, and join the file system to the Simple AD domain.
- Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory with a one-way forest trust to the on-premises domain, and join the file system to the managed directory.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Join the file system directly to the existing on-premises domain as a self-managed Active Directory, using the domain's DNS servers and a service account.

**Deciding phrases.** "existing accounts", "the domain controllers are reachable from the VPC", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Employees keep their on-premises accounts, and the domain controllers are reachable over Direct Connect. An FSx for Windows File Server file system can join an [existing, self-managed Active Directory domain](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed), on premises or in the cloud, so the direct join adds no directory to run. [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) AD Connector or Simple AD.

**Why not.**

- "Create an AD Connector directory that points to ...": [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) AD Connector or Simple AD, so the file system cannot join the domain through an AD Connector directory.
- "Create a Simple AD directory in the VPC, ...": [Amazon FSx does not support](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported) Simple AD, and a copy of the user accounts is a second directory that the company keeps in sync.
- "Create an AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory with ...": It works through a [one-way forest trust relationship](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-resource-forest-one-way-trust), but the company then runs and pays for a second directory, which adds overhead.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company has no Active Directory and wants AWS to run one" instead: create AWS Managed Microsoft AD, because you can [integrate your Amazon FSx file system](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed) with it.

**Takeaway.** FSx for Windows File Server joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or your self-managed domain directly; AD Connector is not an option.

**Review.** [FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB shares that join your Active Directory](2-deep.md#fsx-for-windows-file-server-serves-smb-shares-that-join-your-active-directory-3-min)

</details>
